title: Dungeon Dive Synth - The Sounds You Hear
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3nGph8PX2-Q

Viewers kept asking what the channel's intro music is made on, so Daniel (@dungeondive) answers with a phone camera pointed at a synthesizer the size of a playing card. Around ninety per cent of everything you hear on the Dungeon Dive comes out of a Teenage Engineering OP-1 — and, he cheerfully warns, so does the audio in this video, recorded off its tiny built-in speaker.

The demonstration is mostly the four-track tape machine, which simulates reel-to-reel closely enough to be abused. He plays back the trailer music from his solo RPG series — written entirely on this box — then bends the tape with a knob to introduce wow and flutter, performs a tape stop, runs it backwards, and scrubs through it by hand.

From there, a tour of the rest: a synth engine holding eight presets, a drum engine, a sampler and several sequencers. He walks through the digital engine, a four-operator FM engine he traces to the Yamaha DX7 and rates as the best-sounding of the lot, and a pulse engine, explaining volume versus pitch envelopes and the single LFO along the way — modulate pitch and you get vibrato, modulate volume and you get tremolo. The strangest feature gets the last word: an onboard FM radio you can sample, which produced several of the short experimental stings he plays.

He signs off promising more short cues written for the solo RPG series.

----

Daniel writes his own fifteen-second stings rather than reaching for a library track. How much does original music change how a channel or a game table feels to you?
